hero.name: Bijoy
hero.who: a 34-year-old vegetable farmer near Bardhaman whose days blur between fields and phone orders

story.b: Bijoy grows vegetables on his family's land near Bardhaman. Two years ago he started selling directly to apartment buyers in Kolkata through WhatsApp orders, and business is good. But his days have turned into a blur. He is in the fields by five, phone buzzing in his pocket. He packs crates of brinjal and gourd while talking to buyers. He eats his lunch of rice and fish while replying to messages. He drives to the truck depot answering calls at every signal. One night his wife asks what he ate for lunch, and he cannot remember. Earlier, his daughter showed him a drawing of their pond. He said nice without really looking at it.

ask.q: Bijoy cannot remember his own lunch or really see his daughter's drawing. What would help him most?
o: Take a long holiday far away from the farm
Bring calm attention into the ordinary moments of his normal day
Hire help so he can fit even more into a day
ask.why: A holiday helps for a week, and then the blur returns. Doing even more only speeds it up. The real shift is learning to be present in the ordinary moments he already has, like meals, chores and time with his daughter.

chapters.take: Presence is not saved for holidays. It lives in ordinary moments.

story.b: Bijoy decides to try one small thing. When he packs the crates in the morning, his phone goes on the shelf in the shed. He simply packs. He feels the weight of each brinjal, the smooth skin of the gourds, the cool damp of the jute sacks. He notices bruised ones he would have missed before and sets them aside for home. It takes almost no extra time. That week, buyers send fewer complaints about damaged vegetables. At lunch he tries the same thing, eating without the phone, tasting the mustard in the fish curry. For the first time in months, he remembers clearly what he ate, and the afternoon somehow feels less rushed.

ask.q: Bijoy's wife folds laundry while watching a serial and scrolling her phone, and she feels drained. What could help?
o: Fold faster so the chore ends sooner
Add music as well, to make it more fun
Just fold, with full attention, letting the chore itself be calm time
ask.why: Rushing or piling on more input keeps the mind scattered, so the chore feels like a burden to escape. Doing just one thing with full attention turns even a boring task into a small, calm practice, and the day feels less hurried.

chapters.take: Do one thing at a time, and even chores can become calm.

story.b: One evening at the depot, the Kolkata truck is two hours late. Three buyers are calling, one after another, and one of them is angry. Bijoy feels the heat rising in his chest, his thoughts racing in every direction at once. He stops beside a stack of crates. He breathes in slowly and knows he is breathing in. He breathes out slowly and knows he is breathing out. Three times. He feels his feet on the dusty ground and hears the crickets beyond the depot wall. His mind settles a little. Then he calls each buyer back, one at a time, explains clearly, and promises a small discount on the next order. Nobody shouts.

ask.q: The truck is late, three buyers are calling, and Bijoy's mind is racing. What should he do first?
o: Pause and follow a few slow breaths, then handle one call at a time
Answer all three calls together to save time
Switch off his phone until the truck arrives
ask.why: Juggling every call with a racing mind invites mistakes and sharp words, and switching off simply avoids the problem. A few conscious breaths bring his mind and body back together, so he can handle each call calmly and clearly.

chapters.take: When your mind scatters, a few slow breaths can bring you back.

story.h: A half smile in the queue
story.b: Bijoy starts experimenting with a soft half smile. Not a grin, nothing fake, just letting his face relax a little at the corners. He tries it first thing in the morning, before reaching for his phone. He tries it in the long queue at the fertiliser shop in town, where he usually stands tense and impatient. He tries it when a buyer haggles hard over the price of tomatoes. He notices that his jaw, which he did not know was clenched, loosens. His shoulders drop. Sometimes his mood follows. Once, in the queue, the old man ahead of him turns around, sees his face and smiles back. They talk about the rain the whole way to the counter.

ask.q: Waiting in a long queue at the bank, Bijoy feels irritation rising. Which small practice fits best?
o: Complain to the person behind him to let it out
Relax his face into a gentle half smile and breathe
Keep checking the time to see how much he has lost
ask.why: Complaining and watching the clock feed the irritation and tighten the body further. A soft half smile is not fake cheer, just a way of easing the face, and as the face relaxes, the body and mood often begin to follow.

chapters.take: A gentle half smile can ease your face, and your mood may follow.

story.b: Bijoy has walked the raised edges between his fields thousands of times, always checking something: the water, the pests, the time. One evening after the last order, he walks them for no reason at all. Slowly. He lets each step match his breath. He feels the soft earth give a little under his feet, the cool air coming off the pond, the sound of frogs starting up. He is not going anywhere. For five minutes, he is simply walking. The next evening his daughter asks if she can come. She walks slowly beside him, copying his steps very seriously. It becomes their evening habit, ten quiet minutes before dinner, and both of them sleep better for it.

ask.q: Bijoy's friend says walking only matters if it gets you somewhere or burns calories. What does this idea suggest?
o: He is right, so every walk should have a target
Walk faster so the walk counts as exercise too
A slow walk with attention on each step can calm the mind, with no destination needed
ask.why: Treating every walk as a task keeps the mind busy planning and counting, and speeding up turns it into exercise, which is fine but different. Walking slowly with full awareness of each step and breath is its own calm practice and needs no destination.

chapters.take: Sometimes the whole point of walking is simply to walk.

story.b: Packing one morning, Bijoy holds a ripe tomato and, for once, really thinks about it. The seed came from a shop in Bardhaman town. The water came from the canal and the rain. His father taught him how to stake the plants. Labourers from the next village helped harvest them. Rafiq, the truck driver, will carry them through the night. A family in Salt Lake will cook them in a curry tomorrow. Bijoy is one small link in a long chain. That afternoon, a buyer messages to complain about one bruised tomato. Instead of feeling attacked, he sees her as part of the same chain. He apologises warmly and adds two extra tomatoes next time.

ask.q: A Kolkata customer complains that one tomato in her crate was bruised. How might seeing connections shape Bijoy's reply?
o: He sees her as part of the same chain he belongs to, and replies kindly with a fix
He reminds her that farming is hard and she should be grateful
He ignores the message, since one tomato does not matter
ask.why: Seeing that she, the driver and he are all linked softens the line between seller and complainer, so kindness comes naturally. Lecturing her about gratitude pushes her away, and ignoring her breaks the chain of care that brought the tomatoes to her table.

chapters.take: Seeing how everything connects makes gratitude and kindness come naturally.

story.b: Some weeks later, the orders are as busy as ever. Bijoy still wakes at five and still drives to the depot most evenings. But the days no longer vanish. While packing, his phone stays on the shed shelf. When the truck is late, he breathes before he calls anyone. He half smiles in queues and walks the field edges with his daughter before dinner. Her drawings are now pinned on the wall of the shed, and he can describe every one. One night his wife asks, half teasing, what he ate for lunch. Bijoy grins. Posto, rice, and a green chilli from the third row of the field, he says. He remembers it all.

chapters.take: He did not slow his work down. He simply started being there for it.
